input.narrative:
The last stone goes in at dusk, and you set your palm flat against it to feel the mortar still warm from the day's sun. **Three years.** Three years of hauling granite up from the quarry carts, of chipping and fitting and cursing the tide when it undercut your footings in the night, and now the harbour wall of your town curves complete from the fish-market steps to the old lighthouse rock, sealing the water into a calm green bowl. Gulls wheel overhead, indifferent to the achievement. Somewhere below, the evening boats are nosing in against a swell that, for the first time in a generation, doesn't slam them against the quay.

You straighten, your back aching in that particular deep way that only a mason's back aches, and wipe grit from your hands onto a leather apron gone the colour of dried blood from years of red clay dust. Your knuckles are scarred white in a dozen places, your forearms roped with muscle earned one stone at a time. You are not a young man anymore. This wall may be the last great thing you build.

"Ajax!" a voice calls, and you turn, half-expecting to see one of the quarry boys — until you remember there are three of you in this town who answer to that name, and this voice belongs to none of them but the one who has watched you work every single day of the last three years. Ajax the guard comes striding along the new stone, spear resting easy in the crook of his elbow, the harbour breeze tugging at the horsehair crest of his helmet. He is broad where you are wiry, younger by a decade, with a soldier's watchful eyes that have grown, over these three years, into something closer to friendship than duty.

"It's done," he says, stopping beside you, looking not at you but at the wall itself, running the length of it with something like awe. "By the gods, mason. It's actually done." He raps his knuckles against the stone as if he still doesn't quite believe it will hold.

"It'll hold," you say, though your voice comes out rougher than you mean it to — from dust, or from the strange hollow feeling of finishing something this large. "Storm season will tell us for certain, but it'll hold."

Ajax the guard laughs, a short bark of relief, and claps you on the shoulder hard enough to rock you on your feet. "The harbourmaster's putting on a feast tonight. Whole town's coming down to the wall-head. Even," he adds, lowering his voice with a grin, "that sail-selling namesake of yours is closing up shop early for it. Imagine that — three Ajaxes in one town, and not one of us can afford to miss free wine."

You manage a tired smile at that, the old joke never quite wearing thin. But even as you look out past him, past the torches already being lit along the quay, you notice something that catches in your chest like a snagged hook: out past the harbour mouth, where your wall's shadow ends and the open sea begins, a ship rides at anchor that was not there this morning. No lanterns lit aboard her, no flag you recognize snapping at her mast, just a dark hull sitting low and still against the reddening water, watching the town the way a wolf watches a flock through a fence.

"Ajax," you say slowly, nodding toward it. "Whose ship is that?"

The guard's grin falls away. He follows your gaze, and his hand tightens on his spear.

Head straight down to the quay to get a closer look at the strange ship
